sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content:
Global equity markets delivered a sharply divergent June, with the defining macro event — the US-Iran peace framework signed on June 18 — collapsing Brent crude from above **$100/bbl** to **$75.02/bbl** and catalysing a historic rotation away from the AI-driven technology complex that had dominated April and May. The S&P 500 declined **2.0%** to **7,449.36**, the Nasdaq Composite fell **3.2%** to **26,213.72**, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average surged **2.4%** to an all-time record of **52,319.20** — crossing **52,000** for the first time in history — as institutional capital rotated decisively from mega-cap growth into cyclicals, industrials, and value names that benefit most from energy normalisation.

European markets outperformed materially: eurozone CPI fell to **2.8%** in June from **3.2%** in May, and the DAX and CAC 40 rallied to new multi-month highs even as sterling weakened to a 7-month low near **1.32** following UK Prime Minister Starmer's resignation. The Nikkei 225 surged to successive all-time highs mid-month before AI overinvestment concerns triggered sharp late-month volatility. For the full second quarter, the S&P 500 advanced **16%** and the Nasdaq **20%** — their best quarterly performance since Q2 2020 — underscoring the historic magnitude of the AI-driven, geopolitical-resolution trade that defined the first half of 2026.

sections.title: Your Must-Know Market Themes
sections.content: Four key themes that shaped markets this month:
themes:
US-Iran Peace Framework Ends the Oil Shock -- On June 18, the United States and Iran signed a framework agreement mediated by Pakistan's Prime Minister to end hostilities; Iran committed to immediately reopening the Strait of Hormuz, and the US agreed to lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, releasing an estimated **14 million barrels per day** of previously restricted global supply back to market expectations. Brent crude fell approximately **8%** in the days following the announcement, continuing a decline that had already begun on a surge in Gulf exports in early June, before settling at **$75.02/bbl** at month-end — a collapse of **27%** from the month's open near **$100/bbl** and **$37/bbl** below the early April war-peak of **$118/bbl**. The IEA's June report characterised the deal as the biggest breakthrough in negotiations since the conflict began, while cautioning that full export normalisation may take until September or October given prolonged demining and unresolved transit arrangements.

The supply normalisation carries profound second-order macro implications: eurozone CPI fell to **2.8%** in June (from **3.2%** in May), US headline inflation expectations moderated meaningfully, and central banks across the developed world gained policy flexibility they had lacked under elevated energy prices. The immediate market sequencing was textbook: oil producers' equity guidance was marked sharply lower, rate-sensitive sectors re-rated on disinflation signals, and cyclical industries with high energy input costs — airlines, chemicals, transportation — rallied materially. The peace deal was the single most consequential macro catalyst of Q2 2026.

Sector Rotation: Tech Retreats, Cyclicals Lead -- June 2026 marked the clearest US equity leadership regime shift of the year, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) and mega-cap technology names giving back near-term gains after the SOX's extraordinary **87.8%** Q2 advance — its best quarterly performance since inception in 1994. The Nasdaq Composite fell **3.2%** to **26,213.72** as 'AI overinvestment' concerns — the worry that hyperscaler capex commitments are running ahead of near-term monetisation capacity — combined with a hawkish FOMC signal to compress technology sector multiples. The Dow Jones Industrial Average simultaneously crossed **52,000** for the first time in history, rising **2.4%** to **52,319.20** as industrials, financials, energy-transition names, and consumer staples attracted the capital rotating out of growth.

The June payrolls print of **57,000** versus **113,000** expected reinforced the rotation thesis: a softening labour market supported cyclicals by reducing the probability of a runaway tightening cycle while keeping corporate margins broadly intact. By month-end, a larger share of S&P 500 stocks were trading above their 50-day moving averages than at the start of June — a healthy breadth signal suggesting the rotation was broadening market participation rather than redistributing gains within a narrow cohort. Sell-side consensus raised Q2 2026 EPS growth estimates to **23.1%** year-on-year from **18.8%** at end of Q1, reflecting the positive second-order impact of lower energy input costs on earnings trajectories across industrials, consumer, and healthcare — sectors that led June's advance.

Fed's Hawkish Hold Fuels Dollar Rally -- The FOMC voted unanimously **12-0** on June 17 to hold the federal funds rate at **3.50%-3.75%** for the third consecutive meeting, but Chair Warsh's statement delivered a pivotal hawkish shift: easing-bias language was removed from the policy statement, and the updated dot plot showed nine of 18 officials favouring one or two additional rate hikes before year-end, with the median 2026 fed funds projection rising to **3.8%** from **3.4%** in March. The committee cited persistently elevated inflation relative to the **2%** target and a solid pace of economic expansion as the basis for maintaining restrictive policy. The hawkish hold — combined with the fading Middle East risk premium that had previously supported safe-haven currencies — reignited rate-differential flows strongly to the dollar's benefit, driving the DXY up **2.3%** in June to its highest monthly close since March 2025.

The FX market's reaction was broad-based and pronounced: EUR/USD fell **2.2%** from **1.1683** to **1.1422** as diminished ECB rate-hike expectations widened the US-EU rate spread by **17 basis points** on the 2-year; USD/JPY rose from **159.15** to **162.53** as the yen struggled against the persistent US-Japan rate differential; GBP/USD was the worst G10 performer, falling to a 7-month low near **1.32** as the dollar's advance compounded with UK political shock — Prime Minister Starmer's resignation after a by-election defeat — and a contractionary UK composite PMI of **49.4** (a 14-month low). The synchronised G10 dollar advance was the broadest since early 2025 and materially repriced the remainder-of-year rate and currency outlook.

Gold's Historic Q2 Collapse Resets the Commodities Complex -- Gold posted its worst quarterly performance in 13 years in Q2 2026, closing June 30 at **$4,014.56/oz** — down **14%** in June alone and **28%** below its April all-time high of **$5,589/oz**. The triple headwind was textbook in its construction: dollar strength (DXY +**2.3%**) compressed gold's non-yielding appeal in the most impactful single-month DXY advance since early 2025; collapsing oil prices reduced near-term inflation expectations and eroded the inflation-hedge premium; and the removal of the Middle East war premium dismantled the safe-haven bid that had propelled successive record highs through Q1. The sequential reversal — from three months of safe-haven inflows to a quarter ranking as the worst for bullion in over a decade — illustrates how rapidly the macro underpinnings of precious-metal super-cycles can shift when geopolitical catalysts reverse.

Copper, the commodity most closely tied to the AI-infrastructure buildout thesis, retreated from its June 2 record of **$6.63/lb** to close the month near **$5.90/lb**, as AI overinvestment concerns that weighed on semiconductor equities spilled directly into the metal. Commercial hedgers in the CFTC Commitments of Traders remained heavily net short, signalling physical market scepticism that near-term AI copper demand would justify the elevated speculative premium. The structural supply-deficit thesis remained intact — the Copper Development Association estimates a single hyperscale AI facility consumes up to **50,000 tonnes** of copper versus **5,000-15,000 tonnes** for a conventional data centre — but June confirmed that sentiment-driven premiums erode quickly when the macro narrative shifts.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
The S&P 500 declined **2.0%** in June to close at **7,449.36**, snapping a two-month winning streak but leaving the index with a Q2 total return of **16%** — the best quarterly performance for US equities since Q2 2020. The Nasdaq Composite fell **3.2%** to **26,213.72** as the AI momentum trade paused and institutional capital rotated out of crowded large-cap technology positions, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced **2.4%** to an all-time record close of **52,319.20**, crossing **52,000** for the first time in history on June 29. Technology's underperformance was the defining sector story: the Philadelphia SOX Index, which had surged an extraordinary **87.8%** in Q2, gave back near-term gains as 'AI overinvestment' concerns and a hawkish FOMC repriced high-multiple growth valuations. Year-to-date, the S&P 500 remains up  **9.6%** and the Nasdaq **12.8%**.

The June 17 FOMC decision — a unanimous hold at **3.50%-3.75%** — was superficially in line with expectations, but Chair Warsh's removal of easing-bias language and a dot plot showing nine of 18 officials favouring additional hikes was sufficient to shift sentiment in rate-sensitive growth sectors. The median 2026 fed funds projection rose to **3.8%** (from **3.4%** in March), extending the higher-for-longer regime in ways that compressed technology multiples while providing a tailwind to financials via higher net interest margins. Labour market data reinforced the rotation: the June payrolls print of **57,000** versus **113,000** expected, with unemployment holding at **4.2%** and wage growth at **3.5%** year-on-year, provided sufficient softening to support cyclical earnings without reigniting recession fears.

Despite the monthly headline decline, the broader tape was constructive beneath the surface: market breadth improved materially, with a greater proportion of S&P 500 constituents trading above their 50-day moving averages at month-end than at the start of June. Full-year S&P 500 EPS growth forecasts rose to **23%** year-on-year as buy-side models absorbed the positive second-order effects of lower energy costs across industrials, consumer, and healthcare sectors. The rotation from growth to cyclicals was orderly rather than disorderly — a healthy mid-cycle portfolio rebalancing consistent with a broadening economic expansion rather than a recessionary shift.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equities delivered a standout June relative to their US counterparts, with eurozone CPI falling sharply to **2.8%** from **3.2%** in May on the back of collapsing energy prices, repricing near-term ECB rate expectations and removing the most acute headwind facing European corporates. The DAX advanced to **26,500** — up **5-6%** for the month — as Germany's export-oriented industrial base benefited from lower energy costs and improving supply-chain visibility through the reopened Strait of Hormuz. The CAC 40 climbed to **8,508** by June 28, its highest close since late February, while the pan-European STOXX 600 hit a 52-week high in early July, confirming the breadth and durability of the European advance.

The FTSE 100 was the notable European underperformer, weighed by two idiosyncratic UK headwinds: Prime Minister Starmer's resignation following a by-election defeat injected significant political uncertainty into UK fiscal planning, while the UK composite PMI slipped to a contractionary **49.4** (a 14-month low), flagging a potential shallow growth contraction. Sterling's fall to approximately **1.32** — a 7-month low — further pressured unhedged returns, and the FTSE 100 closed the month at **8,500**, its modest advance driven largely by its energy and materials composition rather than domestic demand.

Europe's thematic leadership in June concentrated in materials, industrials, and consumer discretionary — sectors with the greatest exposure to the post-conflict normalisation trade. European defence names, which had been a sustained outperformer across the first half, modestly gave back their geopolitical premium as the ceasefire reduced urgency on rearmament spending timelines. Energy majors (bp, Shell, TotalEnergies) faced significant earnings-guidance headwinds from the oil-price collapse, with 2026 energy-sector EPS estimates marked lower materially through the month. Overall, June confirmed Europe as the primary developed-market beneficiary of the geopolitical resolution trade, and the ECB's rate trajectory repricing provided an additional multiple-expansion tailwind that the Fed's hawkish hold denied to US growth equities.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Japan's Nikkei 225 delivered the most dramatic intra-month trajectory of any major equity index in June, surging in eight consecutive sessions from June 11 to June 22 as the US-Iran peace framework catalysed a powerful unwinding of geopolitical risk premia. The index advanced from **64,000** on June 11 to above **72,300** by June 22 — a gain of *13%** in eleven sessions — as Japanese industrials, trading houses, semiconductor exporters, and energy-intensive manufacturers rallied on the dual tailwind of lower oil costs and improving global supply-chain visibility. The Nikkei's June peak represented its third consecutive month of all-time record highs, with the year-to-date advance extending to approximately **22-24%**.

However, a sharp reversal emerged in the final week of June as 'AI overinvestment' concerns resurfaced, driving the index briefly below **70,000** before a modest stabilisation. Mounting institutional scepticism that hyperscaler capex commitments have run ahead of near-term demand monetisation disproportionately weighed on semiconductor-heavy indices globally, and the Nikkei's elevated AI-chip exposure made it acutely vulnerable to this narrative. The Nikkei closed the month at **70,500** — still representing a monthly gain of **5%** — but analysts flagged that continued volatility was expected into July as the market digests the AI-capex debate.

Mainland Chinese equities were broadly stable, with the Shanghai Composite closing near **4,074** on June 29, supported by targeted fiscal stimulus from Beijing and improving domestic consumption sentiment. The Hang Seng Index underperformed the broader APAC region, closing the month at **22,500**, weighed by persistent property-sector overhang and geopolitical noise around Hong Kong-listed technology names. South Korean and Taiwanese indices gave back some AI-premium gains as the semiconductor sector digested capacity-overbuild concerns, though management guidance from key chipmakers remained broadly constructive on structural demand through 2027 and beyond.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US Dollar Index (DXY) advanced **2.3%** in June — its second consecutive monthly gain and highest monthly close since March 2025 — as the fading Middle East risk premium shifted FX markets back to rate differentials as the primary driver, firmly to the dollar's structural advantage. The hawkish June FOMC, with nine of 18 officials favouring additional hikes and the median 2026 dot plot rising to **3.8%**, materially widened the US rate advantage as European and Japanese yields were broadly stable or declined on disinflation signals from collapsing oil. EUR/USD fell **2.2%** from **1.1683** to **1.1422** over the month, with the pair's failure to sustain above **1.17** in May now appearing structurally significant as ECB easing expectations diminished relative to the US policy path.

GBP/USD was the worst-performing G10 cross in June, declining **1.8%** to a 7-month low near **1.32** as dollar strength combined with a UK-specific political shock — Prime Minister Starmer's resignation after a by-election defeat, with Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham emerging as the frontrunner to succeed him — and a contractionary composite PMI of **49.4** to generate the most acute single-currency underperformance of the month. USD/JPY rose from **159.15** to **162.53** as the yen proved unable to generate a safe-haven bid in an environment where geopolitical risk was receding, and the persistent US-Japan rate differential remained the dominant directional driver despite the Bank of Japan's measured policy normalisation stance.

Commodity-linked currencies (AUD, CAD, NOK) were the principal G10 losers as Brent crude's **27%** monthly collapse stripped away the energy-export premium that had supported these currencies throughout the conflict period. The Canadian dollar and Australian dollar each fell **2-3%** against the dollar, as markets recalibrated fiscal and export revenue assumptions for commodity-exporting economies. The broader EM FX basket held up relatively well as the inflation normalisation narrative supported emerging market local-currency debt, partially offsetting equity-flow headwinds from dollar strength across higher-beta EM crosses.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
June 2026 will be defined in commodity market history as the month the war premium was systematically extracted from global energy prices. Brent crude collapsed from **$100/bbl** at the start of the month to **$75.02/bbl** at the June 30 close — a decline of **27%** that ranks among the largest monthly dollar-price drops in the benchmark's history. The US-Iran framework agreement (June 18) directly addressed the structural overhang, but prices had already been retreating from highs in early June on a surge in Gulf exports, accelerated IEA government stock releases, and modestly weaker demand; the deal delivered the decisive downside catalyst that fundamentally re-rated the geopolitical risk premium. WTI crude tracked **$3-5/bbl** below Brent, settling near  **$70/bbl** at month-end, with crude's trajectory toward pre-conflict levels raising material questions about 2026 guidance for major oil producers.

Gold delivered its worst quarterly performance in 13 years in Q2 2026, closing June at **$4,014.56/oz** — down **14%** in the month alone and **28%** below the April all-time high of **$5,589/oz**. The simultaneous unwinding of three pillars that had supported gold's historic 2026 bull run — geopolitical war premium, inflation-hedge demand, and haven flows — created an unusual degree of downside conviction. Gold hovered near the psychologically significant **$4,000/oz** level in late June, with institutional conviction in J.P. Morgan's end-year target of **$6,000/oz** meaningfully challenged by the magnitude of Q2's decline.

Copper retreated from its June 2 record high of **$6.63/lb** to close the month near **$5.90/lb**, as the AI overinvestment debate that weighed on semiconductor equities spilled over into the metal most closely associated with the AI data-centre buildout theme. Physical market participants — net short according to the latest CFTC Commitments of Traders — provided limited support, with commercial hedgers signalling scepticism that near-term AI copper demand would justify the elevated speculative premium. The structural case for copper remained compelling given that hyperscale AI facilities consume up to **50,000 tonnes** of copper versus **5,000-15,000 tonnes** for conventional data centres, but June confirmed that sentiment-driven commodity premiums can erode rapidly when the macro narrative pivots.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
US Treasuries rallied counter-intuitively through June despite the Fed's hawkish hold, as Brent crude's **27%** monthly collapse materially reduced near-term inflation expectations and allowed the long end to rally even as the FOMC signalled an elevated terminal rate. The 10-year Treasury yield declined from **4.55%** in early June to **4.38%** by June 26, while the 2-year yield fell from **4.17%** to **4.07%** — a modest bull-steepening dynamic reflecting market scepticism that the Fed would follow through on its hike signalling given the softening labour market (June payrolls: **57,000** versus **113,000** expected) and substantial disinflation from collapsing oil. The FOMC's unanimous hold at **3.50%-3.75%** and dot plot showing nine of 18 officials favouring additional hikes created an unresolved policy fork that markets have priced cautiously, with near-term curve flattening pressure capped by the inflation-expectations tailwind from energy.

European sovereign bonds outperformed US Treasuries on a total return basis as ECB rate expectations declined more sharply on the Eurozone disinflation data (**2.8%** CPI in June) and the energy-price tailwind. German Bund yields fell materially in June, widening the US-EU sovereign spread by **17 basis points** on the 2-year — the key arithmetic behind EUR/USD's **2.2%** monthly decline and the driver of persistent carry flows favouring the dollar across the G10 spectrum. European peripheral spreads tightened modestly as the macro improvement narrative supported southern European fiscal outlooks.

Credit markets were broadly well-supported despite the rates volatility: investment-grade spreads tightened modestly as lower input costs, improving corporate earnings trajectories (Q2 EPS growth estimates rising to **23%** YoY), and the geopolitical resolution underpinned issuer creditworthiness. High-yield outperformed, with leveraged issuers in energy, industrials, and consumer sectors benefiting most from the post-conflict normalisation macro. The US Aggregate Bond Index delivered a positive total return for the month as the Treasury rally more than offset income shortfall, providing a welcome reversal from the negative total returns that had characterised prior hawkish-hold months.
